text.p: Flags flew at half-mast across Ukraine on Saturday as thousands gathered across the country to commemorate the blast 11 years ago at the Chernobyl power station, the world's worst nuclear accident.

Ceremonies to remember those who died in the explosion on April 26, 1986 and its aftermath took place at the site, in the capital, Kiev, just 100 km (60 miles) from the still-operating nuclear plant, and in other parts of the former Soviet republic.

About 5,000 people began an all-night vigil at precisely 1.24 am (22.24 GMT), the moment when staff at Chernobyl lost control of the reactor, in Slavutych, a town 35 km (22 miles) from Chernobyl built to house workers relocated after the accident.

Weeping women lit candles and placed flowers on a monument dedicated to their dead colleagues. Ukrainian authorities estimate some 4,300 died in Chernobyl's wake and several thousand more, including many children afflicted with radiation-related illnesses, continue to suffer.
Over the weekend, tens of thousands of people across the former Soviet Union are marking the memory of the radioactive cloud that spread over Europe and blighted millions of lives.

In neighbouring Belarus, the anniversary has fuelled protests against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko. Thousands of anti-Lukashenko demonstrators were expected in the capital Minsk on Saturday afternoon, in a repetition of last year's protest.

Downwind from Chernobyl, Belarus was very badly affected by the explosion, which blew the reactor's roof off. On Friday, local authorities announced they had opened a case against extremists planning a coup attempt.
Eleven years on, a lack of cash is hampering the efforts of the Soviet successor states to deal with Chernobyl's legacy.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin promised on Saturday the state would continue to care for those who suffered.

He paid tribute to the "liquidators", power workers and soldiers, some of them conscripts, who were sent in to clean up the mess and seal off the flow of deadly gases. Exposed to massive doses of radiation, many died or are dying.
"This disaster cost and continues to cost human lives," Yeltsin said in an official written statement.

"But the scale of the tragedy could have been immeasurably greater if it were not for the bravery and selflessness of those who, without care for their health or sparing their strength, worked to liquidate the consequences of the disaster."
Yeltsin's predecessor in the Kremlin, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, hushed up the disaster for days, aggravating its impact on civilians.
Western areas of Russia, close to the Ukraine and Belarus borders, have an incidence of cancers and other diseases which is many times greater than elsewhere in the country.
Ukraine has drawn up a plan with the Group of Seven leading industrialised Western countries to stabilise the crumbling sarcophagus built around the fourth reactor after it blew up.

President Leonid Kuchma has promised to close down the remaining reactors completely by the year 2000 in return for $3.1 billion of Western credits. The G7 is expected to decide on funding arrangements for the plan at its June summit.

Ukrainian estimates show about two million of its 52 million people live in contaminated areas around Chernobyl, including 479 people who have returned voluntarily to live in the 30-km (19-mile) exclusion zone around the nuclear site.
Nuclear experts say the entire zone should remain uninhabited for the next three centuries.
